newsitem.title: KENYA: A PARALYSED WORLD DEFERS ACTION ON ZAIRE.
newsitem.headline: A PARALYSED WORLD DEFERS ACTION ON ZAIRE.

text.p: A blur of international meetings and words is masking the fact that no power capable of saving 1.2 million refugees scattered in eastern Zaire has given them a single cup of water, let alone a foreign protection force.

Not only impoverished Africa, but the world, appears largely paralysed by the latest crisis in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa because of bad memories in Somalia and from the Rwanda genocide.

"It's a shame, in the strongest terms. But the pattern has been clearly established. The West is willing to give money for someone else to clear up a mess but it will not send white bodies," said a U.N. official.
"It's something to do with the self-obsession of the 1990s."
Diplomats in Nairobi said even with U.S. elections over it was clear the world's superpower is unwilling to send troops for an international force to bring order to eastern Zaire.

And without the military lead of the United States, which dragged the United Nations as a force into Somalia in 1993, it appeared that France would have difficulty persuading enough Western allies to intervene in the Great Lakes region.

Its allies, and arch regional enemy Rwanda, are well aware of the results of France's Operation Turquoise military intervention from eastern Zaire into Rwanda in 1994: safe havens for Hutus, many of whom took part in the genocide of up to a million Tutsis.

Lives were saved by Operation Turquoise but these people including Hutu extremists only fled over the border into eastern Zaire and helped fill the refugee camps which the international community has paid $1 million per day to support ever since.
"We have learned nothing at all since we did nothing in Rwanda in 1994 during the genocide," said a U.N. aid official.
"We spent more than a billion dollars in Rwanda to clean up after something which was the result of a political crisis. But no one did a thing to prevent it happening in the first place."

"It's not necessarily just because it's Africa. You don't really see people lining up to go into Afghanistan. The Europeans had something to prove in the former Yugoslavia. But no one has anything left to prove in Africa, except France," he added.

The United States, in particular, had been balking at the cost of keeping the refugees in Zaire. At the start of the Tutsi rebellion there it even hinted it would be a good thing as it would end the refugee problem by driving them back into Rwanda.

Aldo Ajello, European Union special envoy to the Great Lakes region, was positive at a news conference on Wednesday that a lot was being done. But in essence it added up to the need for more meetings so the world could decide exactly what it could do.

EU countries had to meet to "harmonise" their views and to "harmonise" their position with the United Nations. In the meantime African envoys should be sent to Zaire to persuade it to accept a rebel ceasefire and a neutral force.
Ajello reflected the new order of international involvement in Africa's crises, a perception in the West that Africa should do more to clean up bloodbaths in its backyard with some external funding.
He strongly backed the result of a Nairobi summit on Tuesday of African leaders, who essentially threw the thorny problem of setting up a foreign force back to the U.N. Security Council.
He said the Security Council failed to discuss the Zaire crisis formally on Tuesday night because it was waiting for the results of the Nairobi summit, which Zaire had refused to attend.

Ajello stressed the importance and future role of the grouping of regional states, which took up the Zaire problem at the talks in Nairobi having clamped sanctions on neighbouring Burundi in July in retaliation for an army coup.
"This group has been able to react quickly," the envoy said.

"We never saw anything (in Africa) like that...This should be preserved, this capital, which the African countries should keep using, and we (the West) should just support them and provide assistance."
But African leaders are very wary of sending in just their own troops precisely because it would let the West off the hook of humanitarian disasters and would set an expensive precedent.
On the Zaire problem, the same regional states who agreed to deal with Burundi by isolating it, are too split over the Hutu-Tutsi rivalry to avoid being opposed by one side or the other.
"They sent the ball back into the United Nations' court, but not only to tell the powerful countries they must take the lead in this crisis," said a senior African diplomat in Nairobi.
"The countries of Africa are too divided on the (Hutu-Tutsi) issue and almost any African national contingent would be considered to be biased by one group of another," he added.
